10 · Q4 Pulse 3: full coding of the first messages

What did people ask the AI for, and about which health subject, in their first real message?

Denicia Aragon Espinosa

November 09, 2026

In short

  • Every one of the 52 included first messages was coded with the frozen codebook (version 5), by 3 independent AI coders.
  • The most common requests were “Why is this happening to me?” (37%) and “General facts about health” (29%), followed by “How do I handle this problem, or is it safe?” and “Should I see a doctor or get care?” (19% and 8%).
  • The most common health subject was Bones, joints and muscles (9 messages).
  • The 3 coders gave exactly the same labels on all 52 messages (Fleiss’ κ = 1.0). That shows the codebook is applied consistently; it does not prove the labels are right (see Agreement).
  • All 335 of 335 evidence quotes were found word for word in the messages.
  • 2 messages were flagged, and you (the analyst) decided both. In each, the coders all agreed, but their label clashed with an earlier decision. All counts and charts use the labels after your review.
  • Update (request codebook v6, 2026-11-09): request wording anywhere in the message now counts, and a bare symptom or an own pasted result counts as an implied request. 0 of the 9 messages that were “Shared information, no question asked” moved to a request type (3 new independent coders, ? = 1.0). See Update: implied requests.
  • Your partly filled hand-coding sheet matches the final topic for 6 of 8 messages (κ = 0.71) and the exact set of request types for 3 of 9 (κ = 0.29).

What was done, and why

The codebook was locked before coding. Step 09 froze the codebook (version 5) and saved a “fingerprint” (a SHA-256 hash) of every file. Before coding, the script re-checked the fingerprints and got: “all frozen files match their fingerprints”. So the coders used exactly the codebook you approved. The fingerprints are saved in run_record.json, for example:

tibble(file = names(record$frozen_file_sha256), sha256 = unlist(record$frozen_file_sha256)) |>
  filter(file %in% c("request_codebook.md", "topic_codebook.md", "topic_list_rules.md")) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(file = "Frozen file", sha256 = "Fingerprint (SHA-256)") |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(15))
Frozen file Fingerprint (SHA-256)
request_codebook.md a03e21980e229a3fa65eb81a3018415e04082fea58705acd1380d61037dc0bc3
topic_codebook.md 110f9dcee92966b3d78d3eb9f367336aff3cf9dbe6fe9a820120a290ac5d3375
topic_list_rules.md 1c9d6a33f5d38bddc11430abe79a79da03f34b76cb98b32f75ffa28c42b39e74

Which message was coded. For each person, their first real message (the unit-of-analysis rule in the codebook): 52 chats, with the homework chat excluded and names already replaced by [NAME]. In 3 chats the first message was only a greeting or a one-word reply, so the next real message was used. In 5 chats the AI’s earlier turn was shown as labelled context, only so the message could be understood.

Who coded. 3 AI coders, each started fresh, with no memory of earlier steps. Each coder:

  • saw only the frozen codebook and the messages, never the labels from the drafting passes, the pilot or step 07;
  • got the messages in its own shuffled order (fixed seeds 10101, 10102, 10103, so the run can be repeated);
  • gave every type of request that applied (more than one is allowed) and one primary health topic;
  • backed every code with a word-for-word quote, a confidence rating (high, medium or low) and an “unclear because…” note when the definitions did not settle the case.

How the final label was chosen. A label is kept when at least 2 of the 3 coders gave it (a majority). Messages where the coders split, or where their label clashed with an earlier decision of yours, were flagged for you. You reviewed the flags as the analyst, and your decisions are applied on top of the coders’ labels (see Messages you reviewed). The coders’ own labels are kept next to the final ones in the Excel file, so nothing is lost.

All prompts, inputs and raw coder answers are saved in output/10_code-first-messages/coders/.

Main result: what people asked for

req_main <- main |>
  mutate(is_none = code == "NONE",
         label = factor(plain_label, levels = rev(plain_label)))
p_main <- ggplot(req_main, aes(pct_messages, label, fill = is_none)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = ci95_low, xmax = ci95_high), height = 0.25, linewidth = 0.8,
                 color = project_colors[["charcoal"]]) +
  geom_text(aes(x = ci95_high, label = paste0(n_messages, " of ", n_msg, " = ", pct(pct_messages))),
            hjust = -0.08, size = 6.5, fontface = "bold", color = project_colors[["charcoal"]]) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = project_colors[["ochre"]], `TRUE` = project_colors[["sand"]]), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, max(req_main$ci95_high) * 1.45),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))) +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = function(x) str_wrap(x, 30)) +
  labs(title = "What did people ask the AI for in their first message?",
       subtitle = paste0("Mostly \"", main$plain_label[1], "\" (", pct(main$pct_messages[1]), ") or \"",
                         main$plain_label[2], "\" (", pct(main$pct_messages[2]), ")"),
       caption = paste0("Base: all ", n_msg, " codable first messages. Each bar: messages with that request, and % = messages / ", n_msg, ".\n",
                        "A message can ask for more than one thing, so the % add up to more than 100%.\n",
                        "Thin lines = 95% CI, Wilson."),
       x = NULL, y = NULL)
p_main

save_fig("main-request-types", p_main, width = 13, height = 7.5)

How to read the thin lines (95% confidence intervals). We only have 52 messages, so each % is an estimate. The line shows the range where the “true” % for people like these probably lies. For example, Why is this happening to me? is 37%, but anything from about 25% to 50% fits the data. When two lines overlap a lot, do not read much into the difference. (They are Wilson intervals, which work well for small samples and small %.)

main |>
  transmute(plain_label, code_name = if_else(code == "NONE", "—", paste0(code, " ", name)),
            n_messages, pct_messages,
            ci = paste0(pct1(ci95_low), " – ", pct1(ci95_high))) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(plain_label = "Kind of help (in plain words)", code_name = "Code in the codebook",
             n_messages = "Messages", pct_messages = paste0("% of ", n_msg), ci = "95% confidence interval") |>
  fmt_percent(pct_messages, decimals = 1) |>
  tab_source_note("A message can have more than one type, so the % add up to more than 100%.") |>
  tab_source_note("\"Explain my test results\" had only 1 message before the v6 update; it was kept by your choice, below the usual 3-message minimum.") |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(18), data_row.padding = px(8))

What this does and does not tell us. The 3 coders agreed on every single decision. That is a good sign that the codebook is clear and gets applied the same way each time. But it is not proof that the labels are correct, for two reasons:

  1. The 3 coders are the same AI model, so they tend to read things the same way, including making the same mistakes.
  2. The codebook’s examples are quotes from these same messages, so many messages were close to an example.

Also, they were not always sure: 67 of 335 codes had medium or low confidence, and the coders wrote “unclear” notes (see What the coders found hard). Your own hand-coding is the real test of whether the labels are right.

Quote check

Every code needed a word-for-word quote from the message. A script then searched for each quote in the message text.

  • Found character for character: 335 of 335.
  • So no code rests on words that are not in the message.

Messages you reviewed

No message had a split vote or a topic without a majority. However, 2 messages were flagged because the coders all agreed but their label clashed with a decision you made earlier. You reviewed both as the analyst:

  • 6a0206ae: the coders gave “Why is this happening to me?” and “How do I handle this problem?”. You set it to “Shared information, no question asked” only. In your words: “whats stressing me and why im anxious is not a why is this happening question at all, its just providing information on what the participant wants to talk about.” The message sets up what they want to talk about, with no cause question, and emotion goes to the later sentiment analysis. (Updated on 2026-11-09: under codebook v6, its later request “what I can do to give myself a better quality of life” now counts, so it is “How do I handle this problem, or is it safe?”; see Update: implied requests.)
  • 69f4ca1a: you accepted the coders’ topic, “Pregnancy and reproductive health”, because two of the four conditions named (PCOS and PMDD) are reproductive. This replaces your earlier decision to leave it under “Diabetes and hormones”.

These are decisions about two labels, not changes to the definitions, so the frozen codebook stays as it is. Both are logged in 10_review_decisions.csv (decided by: analyst).

A suggestion, not applied. To stop this happening again, the “Why is this happening to me?” definition could add one line: “Does not include statements about why someone feels a certain way emotionally (for example ‘why I’m anxious’) when no symptom cause is asked; these go to the sentiment analysis.” This would change the definition, so it would need a new frozen version. It is your call.

Update: implied requests (request codebook v6)

Why. You checked the chats labelled “Shared information, no question asked” and found that some did ask something, later in the message or without a question mark, or simply by describing a symptom. You decided (analyst, 2026-11-09):

  • (a) Request wording anywhere in the message counts, with or without a “?”. For 6a0206ae, “what I can do to give myself a better quality of life” is a request about handling the problem, so it is now “How do I handle this problem, or is it safe?”. Your earlier ruling stays: “why I’m anxious” is not a cause question, so it was not given “Why is this happening to me?” (the new coders did give it; we kept your ruling).
  • (b) A bare symptom or health change of the person’s own counts as an implied “Why is this happening to me?”, and a pasted result of their own counts as an implied “Explain my test results”.

How. The codebook was re-frozen as version 6 (step 09, revisions 25 and 26). Then 3 new independent AI coders (fresh, own shuffled order, the example quotes taken from these 9 messages hidden) recoded the 9 messages with the new rule. They agreed on every message (Fleiss’ ? = 1.0 for the opening group), and all 30 of 30 quotes were found word for word. The result is applied as review decisions, so the coders’ original labels stay in the Excel file.

  cols_width(evidence_quote ~ px(300), edge_case_for_researcher ~ px(300)) |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(15))

Edge cases, and your rulings (2026-11-09) (the coders agreed, but said the rule did not fully settle these):

  • 6929d658 (an email draft): all 3 coders kept it as “Shared information, no question asked”, but they were unsure whether the feelings it describes count as a personal health change. Your ruling: it stays “Shared information, no question asked”, and it is left out of the opening-group charts (base 51; step 13 decision L28). It stays in every other analysis.
  • 67d5d3b7: the message lists symptoms in answer to the AI’s offer to judge how concerning the pain is. Coded as an implied “Why is this happening to me?”. Your ruling: stays in Asking to understand (L29).
  • 69fe1811: a positive change (hair regrowth on a medicine), which may be good news rather than a problem. Coded as an implied “Why is this happening to me?”. Your ruling: stays in Asking to understand (L29).

The 3 request-type differences (6a0206ae now matches, after your review):

  • 6144ea17: you gave “what should I do”; the final label also has “why is this happening”.
  • 69f4ca1a: you gave “health goal”; the final label is “handle this problem”, following pilot edit E6 (supplements for named conditions count as handling a problem).
  • 69f441ce: you gave “handle this problem”; the final label is “general facts” plus “should I see a doctor”.

On topics, the 2 differences are 695be8c6 (you: bones and joints; coders: infections) and 6a638cf5 (you: stomach and digestion; coders: no code, so “Other”).

R1 vs implicit self-diagnosis without a cause question (5f491a49 'I think I may have it') and anxiety 'why I'm anxious' (6a0206ae) is not clearly decided. Testosterone as a fitness goal (69fcf529) vs T6 'testosterone' sign could be clarified.
2 6929d658: long journal-style emotional narrative with no question; R4 is framed around symptoms/health details, so it is unclear whether such messages are R4 or NONE. 66aafcc3: message names no health subject itself; topic depends on AI context. 6a9bb385 and 6a638cf5: imaging/test results spanning several organs (kidney, lung, liver) have no topic code, so they fall to NONE. 69fcf529: T6 lists testosterone, but here it is a fitness goal, so T2 vs T6 overlaps. 6a0206ae: R1 is defined for symptoms; unclear whether asking 'why I'm anxious' counts. 5eec8774: prevention of future harm from an existing condition (fracture risk) is not explicitly placed in R3 vs R6. 6785ddfb: 'How do I know if I have X' with no personal symptoms described sits between R1 and R2. 66c0f464: question addressed to the AI about its own experience has no clear request code.
3 No topic code for heart/chest or kidney/urinary subjects, so chest pain (671a8337), a heart/coronary scan (6a9bb385) and a kidney ultrasound (6a638cf5) fall to NONE. R4 is defined around symptoms/test results; long emotional narratives without a request (6929d658) and follow-up answers to the AI (67d5d3b7) fit it only loosely. Short follow-ups whose topic is only in the AI context (66aafcc3, 6a9bb385, 67d5d3b7) are hard to code from the message alone. R1 is written around physical symptoms; asking why one is anxious (6a0206ae) and coping with stress (R3 vs R6) are not clearly covered. Short general questions that may hide a personal case (6ae359af, 6a983ff0, 6ad69d36) sit between R1 and R2. Questions about the AI's own experience (66c0f464) have no request code. Testosterone as a fitness goal (69fcf529) is ambiguous between T2 and T6. Mixed condition lists (69f4ca1a) need a tie-break when no condition is clearly central.

Common points: an emotional narrative with no question (R4 or none?); short replies whose subject is only in the AI’s earlier turn; and no topic line for heart or kidney subjects (these go to “Other”).

Files

  • scripts/10_code-first-messages/
    • prompts/coding_prompt.md: instructions given to each coder.
    • 10a_prepare_coding.py: checks the frozen codebook and builds each coder’s shuffled input.
    • 10b_check_and_combine.py: quote check, majority vote, flags, agreement, comparisons, tables and Excel file.
    • 10_Q4_3_code-first-messages.Rmd: this report.
  • output/10_code-first-messages/
    • 10_Q4_3_final_codes.xlsx: the final labels with quotes, and all tables (start with the “about” sheet).
    • final_labels.csv, main_request_types.csv, topic_list.csv, review_flags.csv, changes_vs_step07.csv, agreement_*.csv, quote_check.csv, coding_long.csv, coder_feedback.csv, hand_coding_*.csv.
    • 10_change_reasons.csv, 10_extra_review_items.csv and 10_review_decisions.csv: hand-written by the analyst (the reasons, the 2 review questions and your decisions on them).
    • In final_labels.csv and the Excel file, *_coders columns hold the coders’ majority labels and *_final_after_review columns hold the final labels used in this report.
    • run_record.json: codebook fingerprints, seeds and input fingerprint.
    • coders/: prompts, inputs, shuffled orders and raw answers from each coder.
    • figures/: the main chart.
